newsitem.title: USA: Reno rejects special probe of U.S. campaign funding.
newsitem.headline: Reno rejects special probe of U.S. campaign funding.

text.p: Attorney General Janet Reno on Monday rejected demands from Republicans in Congress for an independent investigation into alleged fund-raising abuses by President Bill Clinton's Democratic Party and the White House.

Reno's decision to keep the investigation within her own Justice Department set the stage for a possible political battle with congressional Republicans, who have been clamouring for an independent counsel.

Reno said in letters to Republicans on the House of Representatives and Senate Judiciary committees that a Watergate-style special counsel was not justified to investigate Democratic fund-raising activities to help Clinton in the 1996 presidential campaign.

In other developments on Monday, the White House said 56 major Democratic Party contributors flew on Air Force One as guests of Clinton in 1995 and 1996. It also said Vice President Al Gore gave plane rides to 17 contributors in the same period.

And the Democratic Party released some 10,000 pages of internal documents in what appeared to be an effort in advance damage control. The documents described a master plan to raise $7 million in 1996 campaign funds from Asian-Americans.

Reno, a Clinton appointee and a member of his Cabinet, said the investigation into the fund-raising controversy would continue to be conducted by a Justice Department task force of career prosecutors and FBI agents.
"I can assure you that I have given your views and your arguments careful thought," Reno wrote to the Republicans.
"But at this time, I am unable to agree, based on the facts and the law, that an independent counsel should be appointed to handle this investigation," she said.
Reno said the key requirement under the independent counsel law -- specific, credible evidence that a covered person has committed a federal crime -- has not been met.
Reno rejected the Republican view that a Justice Department investigation would involve conflict-of-interest problems.

The fund-raising controversy so far has involved possible attempts at illegal or improper influence-peddling involving foreign donors, mainly from Asia, as well as U.S. sources in financing the campaign that re-elected Clinton.
Reno said any violations of federal criminal law will be thoroughly investigated and prosecuted, if appropriate, by the Justice Department task force.
Reno vowed to monitor the investigation closely and said she would not hesitate to seek an independent counsel "should future developments make it appropriate."

She said the "mere fact" that employees of the White House and the Democratic National Committee worked closely together during Clinton's re-election campaign does not in itself warrant an independent counsel.

Clinton and Reno have long maintained that an independent counsel was unneeded, even though allegations have continued to mount involving the role of the president, Gore and White House officials in raising campaign funds.

"Our views on this are well known. We believe that the decision on this ought to be based on the law and it's a decision for the attorney general," a White House spokesman said after the announcement of Reno's decision.
In Congress, Senate Republican leader Trent Lott of Mississippi called Reno's decision "inexcusable."

Representative Henry Hyde, the Republican chairman of the Judiciary Committee, said Reno had a "personal and political" conflict of interest in the case and had been under "enormous pressure" from the White House not to appoint an independent counsel.
But Democratic Sen. Patrick Leahy of Vermont defended Reno's record and integrity and he accused the Republicans of politicizing the independent counsel law.
